data.title: Mission
data.body:
• ​Provide quality husbandry and veterinary care to animals

  • Facilitate researchers and students for the humane care and use of laboratory animals in biomedical research and teach ing.

  • Educate and train staff, students and researchers to promote responsible use of laboratory animals for the benefit of mankind.​​​​​

data.title: Salient Features
data.body:
• ​​Veterinary care for all laboratory animals to improve welfare and to minimise the risk of zoonosis.

  • Controlled breeding for laboratory animals for a synchronised and economical population.

  • Controlled temperature and light/ dark periods in animal facility for reproducible results.

  • Separation of different species to prevent interspecies disease transmission and to eliminate the potential for anxiety, physiologic and behavioral changes.

  • Quarantine measures have been adapted to control infections.


​​

data.title: Research
data.body: ​It is mandatory to get approval from the Ethics Committee for Animal Care and Use (ECACU) for any animal based research. After approval, researchers will be able to order animals from the Animal Facility. Researchers must receive training in basic animal care and use prior to project commencement.​

data.title: Education and Trainings

data.title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Metagenomics
data.body: ​Recent studies have highlighted the promise and effectiveness of unbiased metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) approach in detecting a broad range of pathogens within a single comprehensive experiment, unveiling its potential in the diagnosis of infectious diseases. In the current study, we used mNGS to evaluate Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) from 101 children aged 0 months to 18 years, who were admitted to Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH) with suspected meningitis. The Chan Zuckerberg ID (CZID) platform was employed to discern potential pathogenic microorganisms in these samples. mNGS analysis revealed several putative pathogens, including human Beta herpesvirus 5, Rotavirus A and Enterovirus B, which had not been identified by conventional testing methods. Interestingly, rather than observing concordant findings regarding pathogens across clinical diagnosis, culture, and pathogen-calling algorithm (CZID); this study uncovered novel potential pathogens by CZID that had remained undetected by standard clinical methods and CSF culture. Nevertheless, there were also instances of concurrency noticed in outcomes between CZID’s mNGS analysis, culture, and the primary diagnosis. For instance, the clinical diagnosis of enterovirus meningitis and the detection of Enterovirus B by CZID coincided. Similarly, the identification of Micrococcus Species in a CSF culture was in line with the identification of Micrococcus luteus through CZID’s mNGS analysis. This study will contribute to a better understanding of the aetiology of meningitis in the pediatric population of Pakistan with the hope of introducing mNGS as point-of-care testing.​

data.title: Oxford Nanopore Technology Plasma Metagenomics
data.body: ​Recent studies have underscored the potential of plasma metagenomic sequencing using the Oxford Nanopore Technology (ONT) platform in identifying the microbial etiology of sepsis in pediatric patients. In this project, we aimed to evaluate the performance and cost-effectiveness of ONT MinION sequencing in comparison to traditional blood culture. The study involved children aged 1 month to 18 years admitted to the PICU with suspected sepsis. Initial results from two batches, analyzed using the ONT pipeline on the Chan Zuckerberg ID (CZID) platform, revealed the presence of various microbes in sepsis patients that were undetected by conventional blood culture. These findings highlighted the superior diagnostic resolution of mNGS over blood culture, offering more detailed insights into the microbial landscape in sepsis cases. This study also has the potential to inform the cost-effectiveness of implementing ONT MinION sequencing as a diagnostic tool for sepsis management in pediatric populations.​

data.title: Gut Metagenomics
data.body:
​The AMANHI Metagenomics study focuses on investigating the role of the maternal gut microbiome in pregnancy outcomes by comparing microbial diversity between mothers who delivered at term and those who delivered preterm. Using samples from the AMANHI biorepository cohort1, the study aims to identify specific gut microbiome signals that may be associated with term and preterm deliveries. By analyzing the composition and diversity of the maternal gut microbiome, the research seeks to uncover whether distinct differences exist between these two groups and how these microbial patterns may influence pregnancy outcomes. This exploration is critical in understanding the potential link between the maternal microbiome and preterm birth, which could ultimately lead to the identification of new biomarkers or interventions to reduce the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Cohort Profile: The Alliance for Maternal and Newborn Health Improvement (AMANHI) biobanking study. PMID: 34999881; PMCID: PMC8743110.

data.title: MOMI Biorepository Platform: AMANHI Pakistan – Using Multiomics to Investigate Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes (APOs)
data.body:
The Multiomics for Mothers and Infants (MOMI) biorepository platform is focused on addressing adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs) by identifying genetic and biological markers associated with conditions like preterm birth, preeclampsia, stillbirth, and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). Through collaborations with institutions like Stanford University, University of Cincinnati, UCSF and others, the project aims to advance the identification of biomarkers for gestational age and preterm birth—key challenges in the Pakistani population. The MOMI platform supports biobank maintenance and DNA/RNA isolation from AMANHI samples, with a focus on genetic marker identification for preterm birth and maternal selenium's association with gestational age. Additionally, the project seeks to estimate gestational age using genomics, proteomics and metabolic biomarkers and employs a multiomics approach, integrating proteomics, metabolomics, and transcriptomics with machine learning strategies.​

data.title: Asia Pathogen Genomics Initiative APGI
data.body:
Pakistan's genomic surveillance efforts, supported by the Asia Pathogen Genomics Initiative (Asia PGI), focus on enhancing pathogen detection capabilities for public health. With contributions from institutions like the National Institute of Health (NIH) and Aga Khan University (AKU), genomic surveillance programs target specific pathogens such as Polio, Tuberculosis (TB), and SARS-CoV-2. Despite notable progress, the country lacks a comprehensive national plan integrating pathogen genomics into wider surveillance strategies.

The country relies heavily on external donor funding to build short-term capacity, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, which accelerated the establishment of next-generation sequencing (NGS) capabilities. However, long-term sustainability remains a critical challenge, as does the lack of a unified approach for genomic surveillance across various diseases. Supply chain bottlenecks, such as delays in procuring reagents and repairing equipment, further hinder the efficiency of genomic data generation and timely reporting.

General genomic surveillance in Asia reveals several regional patterns:

All 13 participating countries, including Pakistan, conduct in-country next-generation sequencing (NGS). Prioritized pathogens include SARS-CoV-2, tuberculosis, antimicrobial-resistant bacteria, and influenza. Challenges across countries include reliance on external funding, laboratory accreditation gaps, and limited bioinformatics capacity.

In Pakistan, vertical programs exist for specific diseases, but integrated efforts for diverse pathogens and robust strategic planning are essential. Efforts like Asia PGI provide a platform to build capacity, share data, and address barriers, ensuring genomic surveillance contributes to pandemic preparedness and public health interventions effectively.

Pathogen genomic surveillance status among lower resource settings in Asia. PMID: 39317773; PMCID: PMC11445059.

data.title: Global Genomics Surveillance of Pneumococcus Consortium (GPS2)
data.body:
The Global Pneumococcus Sequencing (GPS2) project aims to support sustainable genomic surveillance of pneumococcal pathogens, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where the technology is emerging. By leveraging local genomics labs, GPS2 seeks to enhance capacity for genomic analysis, not only for pneumococcus but for other priority pathogens, thus fostering cost-effective, long-term utilization of genomic technologies. This initiative envisions a self-sustaining model where increased lab use will drive down per-sample costs, ensuring broader access and supporting global infectious disease control efforts. The project will consolidate pneumococcal genomic data to inform on bacterial evolution in response to vaccines, evaluate the current and future efficacy of vaccines, and guide the design of new vaccines.

data.title: Klebnet Consortium and E. coli Sequencing
data.body:
Neonatal sepsis is a leading cause of infant mortality globally, with Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli among the most prevalent bacterial pathogens. In Pakistan, where neonatal sepsis remains a significant health challenge, a genome sequencing project was initiated to better understand the biology, pathogenesis, and antimicrobial resistance of these pathogens in pediatric populations.

At AKU, a comprehensive repository of K. pneumoniae and E. coli isolates was developed, incorporating samples from archived studies (ANISA and SATT trials), ongoing WHO clinical trials (PSBI), and AKU's clinical laboratories across Pakistan. These efforts aim to uncover insights into the genetic diversity, virulence factors, and antimicrobial resistance mechanisms of Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli. This work underscores the critical need for vaccines targeting K. pneumoniae and E. coli, especially as no FDA-approved vaccines currently exist for these priority pathogens. Findings from this study are pivotal for guiding future vaccine development and understanding resistance mechanisms in neonatal sepsis pathogens. Additionally, the establishment of genomic sequencing capacity at AKU marks a significant advancement in tackling antimicrobial resistance and neonatal sepsis in low-resource settings.

data.title: GBS Juno
data.body:
Genomic surveillance of Group B Streptococcus (GBS, Streptococcus agalactiae) is critical for addressing neonatal and maternal morbidity, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) like Pakistan. At AKU, a whole-genome sequencing (WGS)-based study is being conducted in collaboration with the Wellcome Sanger Institute under the Juno Project to investigate the diversity and genetic characteristics of GBS. Vaginal swabs biobanked from the MOMI Ideas Fund study were utilized, providing a unique opportunity to study GBS isolates from pregnant women in peri-urban areas of Karachi.

The study has sequenced and analyzed 31 GBS isolates to date, with additional samples in progress. Initial findings have identified diverse capsular serotypes, genetic markers, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) mechanisms associated with the pathogen. Key analyses include phylogenetic structure determination, serotype switching events, AMR gene profiling, and pan-genome characterization. This data provides critical insights into GBS carriage, disease, and its potential impact on vaccine design.

Despite challenges such as limited local genomic research infrastructure and complex logistics, this ongoing study demonstrates the potential of leveraging existing biobanked samples to inform global health interventions. It also marks significant progress in genomic surveillance capacity at AKU, laying the groundwork for future research on GBS in Pakistan and other LMICs. Findings from this study will contribute to the development of vaccines and targeted health strategies to reduce the global burden of GBS-related neonatal and maternal morbidity.

data.title: Wastewater Surveillance for SARS-CoV-2 in Karachi
data.body:
​

Wastewater surveillance allows the detection of pathogens like SARS-CoV-2, which can signal community-level outbreaks before clinical cases are reported. At AKU, wastewater surveillance was utilized to predict COVID-19 outbreaks in District East, Karachi, Pakistan​.  The study collected 151 raw sewage samples from four sites along the Lyari River between June 2021 and January 2022, with 81.5% testing positive for SARS-CoV-2 RNA. Statistical analysis showed that viral RNA concentrations in wastewater reliably predicted COVID-19 case trends with a lead time of 14 days. Genomic sequencing revealed the dominance of the delta variant until October 2022, with the omicron variant detected in November 2022, ahead of clinical specimen identification. Despite challenges like global supply constraints and the absence of sewage maps, this study demonstrated the effectiveness of wastewater surveillance in low-resource settings and established local capacity for in-house genomic sequencing. Findings were shared in a dissemination seminar attended by national and international health expert1. 

Environmental surveillance for COVID-19 using SARS-CoV-2 RNA concentration in wastewater - a study in District East, Karachi, Pakistan. PMID: 38234701; PMCID: PMC10794106.

data.title: Implementation of Standardized Bioinformatics Practices, Pipelines, and Data Structures in SARS-CoV-2
data.body:
​

In April 2021, our research team received funding from the Public Health Alliance for Genomic Epidemiology (PHA4GE) to enhance local capacity for generating and sharing SARS-CoV-2 viral sequence data. The project aimed to sequence COVID-19 samples and submit the data to public repositories like INSDC (SRA+GenBank, ENA) and GISAID. While Pakistan was impacted by SARS-CoV-2, early viral transmission patterns were not well understood due to limited genomic data. Through this initiative, ~1000 positive COVID-19 samples were sequenced, and ~800 high-quality SARS-CoV-2 genome assemblies were made publicly available. Additionally, Bioinformatics protocols were documented on GitBook, and PANGO lineages were designated on Nextstrain for genomic epidemiology. A Pakistan-specific SARS-CoV-2 tree was also deployed on Nextstrain using local sequencing data from GISAID. This effort enabled near real-time reporting of genomic data to the Ministry of Health and established scalable SARS-CoV-2 genomic analysis capabilities in Pakistan.

data.title: MUMTA Pregnant Women (PW) and Lactating Women (LW) studies
data.body:
​​The MUMTA Pregnant Women (PW) and Lactating Women (LW) studies were community-based, randomized controlled, assessor-blinded trials conducted in peri-urban areas of Karachi, Pakistan, aimed at evaluating the impact of a locally produced Lipid-based Nutritional Supplement (BEP) for Pregnant and Lactating Women.

MUMTA-LW: The LW trial enrolled mothers intending to breastfeed their newborns with mid-upper arm circumference of <23 cm at the time when the infants were 0 to 6d of life. The mothers were randomly assigned to 1 of 3 arms in a 1:1:1 ratio. Lactating mothers in the control arm received standard-of-care counseling on exclusive breastfeeding, nutrition, infant immunization, and health promotion plus iron-folate supplementation until the infant was 6 months old. In intervention arm 1, mothers additionally received two 75 gm sachets of BEP per day. In intervention arm 2, along with the standard-of-care and BEP to the mother, the infant also received 1 dose of azithromycin (20 mg/kg) at the age of 42 days. The primary outcome was infant length velocity at 6 mo. The total sample size was 957 (319 in each arm) along with a single prophylactic dose of Azithromycin for infants, on infant growth over the first six months of life. The trial enrolls lactating women (LW) and their infants within 168 hours of birth, with participants randomized into three arms. Arm A serves as the control, providing standard care including nutritional counseling, breastfeeding support, and essential infant care. Arm B adds a nutritional supplement, with LW receiving two sachets of 75 gm daily for six months, alongside standard care. Arm C combines the nutritional supplement for LW with a single dose of Azithromycin (20 mg/kg) for the infant at 42 days of age, in addition to standard care. The primary aim is to assess the efficacy of the nutritional supplement on infant length velocity, with weight velocity as a secondary outcome. This trial explores whether supplementation and/or antibiotic prophylaxis can enhance infant growth compared to the current standard of care.

MUMTA-PW: The MUMTA-PW  trial enrolled pregnant women with ultrasound-confirmed gestational age (GA) 8-18.·9 weeks on ultrasound scan, who were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1), to one of four groups: control (standard-of-care), BEP alone (10·5 g protein, 400 kcal per sachet, two sachets daily, plus standard-of-care), BEP plus AZ (two doses of 2 g orally at weeks 20 and 28, plus standard-of-care), or BEP plus choline (450 mg orally daily) and nicotinamide (100 mg orally daily) along with standard-of-care. Interventions began at enrollment and continued until birth. using specially developed software and random blocks (size was kept confidential), to either controls (received standard-of-care i.e., provision of antenatal care, skilled birth attendants, nutrition counseling and iron-folate supplements) or the BEP alone group (10.5 grams (gm) protein, 400 kilocalories per sachet, two sachets of BEP supplements along with standard-of-care) or the BEP (similar dose) plus AZ group (two doses of AZ; 2 gm orally at week 20 and 28 of GA) along with standard-of-care or the BEP (similar dose) plus choline and nicotinamide (Choline: daily single oral dose of 450 mg; nicotinamide: daily single oral dose of 100 mg) along with standard-of-care. BEP intervention in all intervention groups as well as choline and nicotinamide in third intervention group were started from the day of enrollment until the birth outcome. The primary endpoint was birth weight among live births, assessed within 72 hours in the intention-to-treat sample (all newborn)1,2.

MUMTA-LW: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03564652

MUMTA-PW: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04012177

Exploring the Maternal and Infant Gut Microbiome (Insights from the MUMTA Trial)

At our cutting-edge research institute, we are pioneering the efforts to understand the intricate relationship between maternal health and the infant gut microbiome through the MUMTA trial. This randomized, case-control study investigates the effects of nutritional supplements - Balance Energy Protein (BEP), Azithromycin (AZ), Choline, and Nicotinamide - on the maternal microbiome before and after pregnancy. Conducted in the peri-urban slums of Karachi, the study aims to improve birth outcomes by providing nutritional support and prophylactic azithromycin to pregnant women.

 With hundreds of metagenomes sequenced and analyzed using advanced machine-learning techniques, our findings have been transformative. Notably, preliminary analyses suggest that certain bacterial populations show significant shifts following the intervention, with both decreases and increases in specific microbiota. However, some relationships, such as maternal antibiotic use and infant microbiome colonization, require further exploration.

This groundbreaking research offers valuable insights into how maternal interventions can shape the gut microbiome, influencing both mother and infant health outcomes. While these results are promising, our work continues as we explore the long-term impacts of microbiome changes on birth outcomes. Our team remains committed to advancing global maternal and infant health through innovative science.

data.title: Experimental Medicine Platform - Maternal Probiotic Intervention to Improve Gut Health
data.body:
The EMP trial aims to assess whether the probiotic Vivomixx1 can modulate maternal microbiota and reduce the effects of maternal environmental enteropathy, a condition that impairs infant growth during the critical first 1,000 days of life. Vivomixx, a well-established probiotic used in thousands of individuals, including pregnant women, has shown potential benefits in various studies. This trial is the first in a series of proof-of-concept interventions designed to generate data that will inform the selection of effective interventions for future large-scale trials. The ultimate goal of these trials is to evaluate the impact of such interventions on birth outcomes and postnatal growth2.

data.title: Impact
data.body:
• ​​Keeping in view the regional spectrum of health needs and pattern of communicable diseases, this was the first purpose-built and fully functional Biosafety Level 3 facility in Pakistan that allowed researchers to conduct work on exotic and potentially lethal bacteria and viruses

  • This lab has also functioned as a preemptive unit to introduce new laboratory techniques that became preferred bio-analytical methods in research and diagnostics at the University Hospital. Till 2004, it was the only facility in Pakistan that could offer Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) testing for tuberculosis. Eventually, the PCR technology was acquired by the Aga Khan University Hospital Laboratory and national labs

  • The only facility that could support testing for anthrax in the 2001 bio-terrorism case at a leading newspaper’s office in Karachi, Pakistan

  • Research Laboratory, Juma Lab regularly back-stops the University Hospital labs for several key tests

data.title: About the Group
data.body:
​Our multidisciplinary ICU research group comprises clinical and academic experts from both adult and pediatric specialties, dedicated to advancing evidence-based resuscitation and critical care practices. Central to our mission is improving rapid response systems and in-hospital cardiac arrest outcomes through comprehensive registries, process evaluations, and innovative strategies. Additionally, we investigate the burden of critical illnesses such as sepsis, ARDS, and critical illness neuromyopathy, while examining short- and long-term ICU outcomes and their underlying contextual factors.

Ongoing projects include establishing an in-hospital cardiac arrest registry, assessing the effectiveness of rapid response teams, studying ARDS and sepsis phenotypes, and evaluating quality of life among post–cardiac arrest survivors. In addition, we examine the role of nutrition and antibiotic stewardship in influencing recovery. 

Through collaborative multidisciplinary expertise and a commitment to equitable care, we work to strengthen critical care delivery, refine resuscitation practices, and improve both survival rates and long-term recovery outcomes for critically ill patients.

Webpage created September 2025

data.title: Aims and Objectives
data.body:
​These are the questions that the group would like to address: 

  • What is the burden of critical care diseases such as sepsis, ARDS, critical care neuromyopathy, etc. in our set up?
  • What are the ICU outcomes (short- and long-term outcomes) and the contextual factors contributing to these outcomes, including interventions that can improve those factors?
  • What are the strategies to mitigate the risk of in-patient cardiac arrest and what processes can be developed to enhance the outcome of in hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA)?
  • The group will work on identification of potential disparities and inequities in critical care.

The following are the objectives of this group:

  1. Develop a comprehensive database to track the prevalence and outcomes of sepsis, ARDS, and other critical illnesses to inform care and policy decisions.
  2. Identify key factors influencing short- and long-term ICU outcomes and develop strategies to optimize recovery and survival.
  3. Implement interventions to prevent in-hospital cardiac arrest and improve survival through better rapid response systems.
  4. Develop accurate digital registries for ICU patients and IHCA to support quality improvement and research.
  5. Identify disparities in access and outcomes and create targeted initiatives to promote equitable critical care.
  6. Conduct research on nutrition, antibiotic use, and post-ICU recovery to enhance patient outcomes and guide clinical practice.

Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation - $499,756
PIs – Asad Latif, Zainab Samad, Adil Haider
Co-P1: Faisal Khan

The purpose of this project is to increase the healthcare system capacity to take care of critically ill patients with COVID-19 in Pakistan. This will be done using a multipronged approach. First, we will train physician, nurses, and paramedical staff in acute critical care patient management with a particular focus on COVID-19. Second, we will help assess existing and newly created ICUs to ensure readiness for care of critically ill and COVID patients, Finally, we will support direct patient care in public sector ICUs using an innovative remote consultation model using existing technologies to help guide local patient management

University Research Council, Aga Khan University
PKR 1,496,110
PI – Shahan Waheed 
Co-P1: Muhammad Faisal Khan

Our study aims to find the differences of delivery of oxygen during direct laryngoscopy utilizing low flow nasal cannula, high flow nasal cannula and compare these with the usual standard of care in which there is no delivery of oxygen during direct laryngoscopy in the Emergency Department. Acquiring a greater understanding of the implications of this technique on patient care by performing a randomized control trial can help clarify its standing in the existing Emergency Department Airway management.

data.title: About the group
data.body:
Emergence and spread of antimicrobial resistance is one of the greatest global threats to health. Low and middle income countries (LMICs) shouldering the bulk of the global burden of infectious diseases are greatly impacted by such resistance. Strong microbiology expertise at AKU enabled it to detect and report resistance trends.

A programme to develop and strengthen capacity for AMR surveillance, containment and diagnosis through public-private partnerships (2006-2010) enhanced expertise, gathered baseline data and established national links and collaborations. Expanded through subsequent projects and programmes this has contributed to establishment of a talented multidisciplinary team.
 
The group includes researchers from the department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine (Section of Clinical Microbiology), Internal Medicine, Community Health Sciences, and Paediatrics and Child Health. Together, these teams have played key roles in studying epidemiology of  adult and paediatric infectious diseases, and in outbreak control. Infectious disease physicians and clinical microbiologists with experience in antimicrobial stewardship and hospital infection control are included. Clinical microbiology is supplemented with molecular skills including use of whole genome sequencing to detect resistance genes.

Our capacity is enhanced by inclusion of expertise in public health, epidemiology and health policy from Department of Community Health Sciences; world leaders in community oriented research of public health importance aimed at informing health policy and with access to well established field sites.

data.title: Aims and Objectives
data.body:
​With established collaborative links with national (including for human and animal health) and international institutions the group links up varied and complementary research approaches for addressing the AMR problem and towards identifying solutions towards its control through:

  • Monitoring and understanding antimicrobial resistance including its molecular basis, transmission and control
  • Using research findings to develop prevention strategies and healthcare intervention
  • Generating evidence to inform public health policy and advocacy for AMR

data.title: Research Themes
data.body:
• Detection of emerging antimicrobial resistance:
    • Review and monitoring antimicrobial resistance trends
    • Understanding genetic basis, molecular mechanism of resistance
    • Early and accurate detection of emerging resistance including using whole genome sequencing to detect resistance gene.
  • Investigation of AMR outbreak:
    • Epidemiology and understanding route of spread of resistance
    • Interventions to control outbreak
  • AMR surveillance:
    • Investigating strategies to improve capacity for quality assured AMR detection at a national level
  • Create advocacy for AMR and AMR control
  • Enhancing laboratory capacity and diagnostics for detection of AMR

data.title: Projects / Studies
data.body:
• ​One of the major challenges in implementing surveillance for antimicrobial resistance is availability of quality assured microbiology. Through Health Security Partners and World Health Organisation supported projects we have been working towards strengthening capacity for drug sensitivity testing in a number of laboratories. This work has been published (https://aricjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13756-017-0260-6). An on-line training course aimed at improving clinical microbiology bench practices in peripheral laboratories in the country is being developed to be available on www.parn.org.pk; a website aimed at sharing information and educational material relating to antimicrobial resistance.
  • To better understand factors contributing to antimicrobial resistance in collaboration with Dr. Johanna Hanefeld and Dr. Mishal Khan from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, we are exploring links between policymakers’ perceptions of antimicrobial resistance and policies for appropriate antimicrobial use in Pakistan.
  • Pathogen surveillance in collaboration with the University of Florida US, provides an opportunity to investigate causes of undifferentiated fever among: patient with rash and arthralgia, bleeding diathesis and neurological symptoms. While the project focuses on surveillance for Arboviruses (Dengue, Chikungunya, West Nile and Japanese Encephalitis), by defining the role of these viral illness, it contributes towards better understanding of the spectrum of pathogens involved in causation of undifferentiated fever (and thus antimicrobial consumption) in our population.
  • Another related One Health project on geographically linking the seroprevalence of WNV in animals and birds with the WN cases identified during the above study has been planned.
  • Detection of carbapenemase enzyme among carbapenem resistant Enterobacteriaceae clinical isolates by modified carbapenemase  inactivation method

data.title: Engagement and Involvement: Public and private
data.body:
• Multidrug resistant Salmonella typhi first identified in the AKU clinical laboratory was sequenced in collaboration with the Sanger Institute (Cambridge UK). The study revealed the emergence of an extensively drug-resistance strain of Salmonella typhi serovar Typhi clone harbouring a promiscuous plasmid encoding resistance to fluoroquinolones and third generation cephalosporins http://mbio.asm.org/content/9/1/e00105-18.long. These findings were shared with the scientific community as well as with the press including through social media.
  • Our recent publication in collaboration with LSHTM discussing opportunities, incentives and barriers to integration of tuberculosis and antimicrobial resistance control programmes https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5840628/ was widely shared on-line and through social media.
  • Consultative meeting on antimicrobial resistance through environmental pathways in Pakistan was held in Karachi in collaboration with the University of Warwick and LSHTM. November 13th -14th 2017. The meeting included a large number of stakeholders from different sectors and was part of a grant awarded to emphasize role of One Health in AMR.
  • Publication in collaboration with Chatham House/LSHTM; Exploring the evidence base for national and regional policy interventions to combat resistance. Lancet. 2016 Jan 16;387(10015):285-95. Was part of a Lancet Series on AMR and thus shared on-line and through social media after its launch; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673615005206?via%3Dihub.
  • Research findings of our study on Challenges and Opportunities in Laboratory capacity building for AMR surveillance in Pakistan were shared in December 2016 in a symposium to highlight AMR situation in Pakistan; Antimicrobial Resistance in Pakistan: Current Situation and Future Approaches; held in collaboration with HSP, Medical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases Society of Pakistan and the Pakistan Academy of Sciences https://www.aku.edu/events/Pages/event-detail.aspx?EventID=440&Title=Anti+Microbial+Resistance+In+Pakistan.
  • As Member Global AMR Surveillance System (GLASS) Collaborative Platform WHO Prof Rumina Hasan has contributed to the following documents:
  • Diagnostic stewardship. A guide to implementation in antimicrobial resistance surveillance sites. WHO/DGO/AMR/2016.3   
  • National antimicrobial resistance surveillance systems and participation in the Global Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance System (GLASS). A guide to planning, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation. WHO/DGO/AMR/2016.4
  • Prof Rumina Hasan also serves as a Member of the Strategic Technical Advisory Group on Antimicrobial Resistance (STAG-AMR) WHO, Geneva.
  • Dr. .Erum Khan, Serves as a country Ambassador for the American Society of Microbiology, she is also member of National Working Group for the development of National Laboratory Biosafety Guidelines initiative of World Health and Government of Pakistan (NIH). Dr. Khan has organized multiple workshops on laboratory biosafety one such workshop titled “Emerging Super Bugs: Standardizing Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing Surveillance and Lab Biosafety” was attended by laboratory staff from all over Pakistan. It provided hands-on training for different methods of Antimicrobial susceptibility testing and interpretation. It received national media coverage and pre and post workshop assessments and outcomes were published in international journal for wider audience. Dr. Khan is also supervisor of one-health fellowship program jointly runned by National Academy of Science –Pakistan and USA
  • Links with the US National Academy of Sciences have also been created through a One Health fellowship awarded in 2016-2017 to Dr Joveria Farooqi. Through this fellowship, additional ties with University of Agriculture, Faisalabad, National Agriculture Research Council, Pakistan and Kenya Medical Research Institute, Nairobi, as well as Washington State University have been set up. Collaborative projects on One Health and AMR transmission through scavenger birds are being planned.
  • Dr. Farah Qamar attended WHO consultation on the use of azithromycin to improve child survival, Geneva and a WHO meeting to discuss epidemiology  and surveillance data to be used by countries for TCV intro decisions and also for TCV use for outbreaks in 2018

data.title: About the Group
data.body: ​The University of Washington, and collaborators at Rockefeller University (NYC), FIOCRUZ (Brazil), IRESSEF (Senegal), KRISP (South Africa), Aga Khan University (Pakistan), and Chang Gung University (Taiwan) were awarded an NIH National Institutes of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID) Centers for Research in Emerging Infectious Diseases (CREID) grant to form the United World for Antiviral Research Network (UWARN) to develop innovative diagnostic reagents, including human viral-neutralizing antibodies and designed proteins that release light when antibodies to the virus are present in the blood (LOCKR technology from IPD). ​

data.title: Aims and Objectives
data.body:
• Build an international capacity laboratory for genomics and surveillance of emerging Viruses in Pakistan.

  • Development of non-cross reactive, species-specific sero-diagnostic for emerging Viruses.

  • Develop a detailed understanding of innate immunity responses captured through RNA transcriptomic to understand the pathogenesis and identification of biomarkers for those at risk for serious sequel of disease.

data.title: Research Themes

  • Mutation analysis of emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants in Pakistan.

data.title: About the group
data.body:
The Biorepository & Omics Group at Aga Khan University drives innovation in maternal, newborn, and child health research by combining population-level biobanking with genomics, multi-omics, microbiome science, and bioinformatics. At the heart of our mission is discovery science, uncovering the biological insights that influence health and disease, and translating these findings into solutions for communities locally and globally. 

In 2013, we launched Pakistan’s first maternal–newborn biorepository under the Alliance for Maternal and Newborn Health Improvement (AMANHI) project in collaboration with WHO. This initiative established the country’s capacity to collect, store, and analyze biospecimens at scale and we continue to strive toward maternal–newborn biorepository under the Alliance for Maternal and Newborn Health Improvement (AMANHI) project, in collaboration with the expanding its impact by enabling systematic investigation of the biological mechanisms underlying maternal and infant health. 

Building on this success, and as members of the Multi-Omics for Mothers and Infants (MOMI) Consortium, funded by the Gates Foundation, we contribute to global efforts to uncover genetic, molecular, and biological markers of adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs). This work aims to improve how risks are predicted, diagnosed, and managed for mothers and babies. 

Our group also leads research within the Experimental Medicine Platform (EMP), focusing on the Maternal Probiotic Intervention to Improve Gut Health trials and the Pregnancy Risk Infant Surveillance and Measurement Alliance (PRISMA) metagenomics sub study, initiatives positioning AKU at the forefront of microbiome research in Pakistan. These projects explore how microbial communities influence maternal, fetal, and infant health, with the goal of translating discovery into innovative interventions that improve outcomes across generations.

Beyond maternal health, we are actively engaged in infectious diseases and pathogen genomics. As part of the Asia Pathogen Genomics Initiative (Asia PGI), we are strengthening Pakistan’s genomic surveillance capacity and enhancing pathogen detection for public health. Our contributions extend to major global projects, including:

  • Wastewater surveillance for SARS-CoV-2
  • Global Pneumococcus Sequencing (GPS2)
  • Genomic surveillance of Group B Streptococcus (GBS)
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae (Klebnet Consortium) & Escherichia coli sequencing projects, investigating antimicrobial resistance in pediatric populations.

COVID-19 Response

During the pandemic, we partnered with the CZBioHub and Public Health Alliance for Genomic Epidemiology (PHA4GE) to enhance Pakistan’s ability to generate and share SARS-CoV-2 sequence data. This work was critical in understanding early viral transmission patterns in the country. https://nextstrain.org/community/AKU-CITRIC-Center-for-Bioinformatics/ncov/Pakistan

data.title: Research Themes
data.body:
​Our research investigates the crosstalk between various risk factors that tip pregnancy biology from healthy adaptation to disease. The framework above guides our studies and research designs.

  • Maternal and Child Health: The aim of our group is to establish biorepository as a scientific field at AKU, with a focus on identifying genetic markers of health and disease relevant to maternal and child populations. Within the maternal population, our goal is to address APOs, such as, preterm birth (PTB), pre-eclampsia, stillbirth, miscarriage, growth restriction and small-for-gestational-age (SGA) births. By identifying these genetic markers, we aim to reduce pregnancy complications, improve maternal well-being and protect the health of future generations.

  • ​Microbiome Science: Beyond human genetics, maternal health is also shaped by microbial ecosystems. The gut microbiome and the reproductive tract microbiome can affect a woman’s health during pregnancy. Changes or imbalances in these microbiomes are linked to APOs. Our aim is to study the gut microbiome with the goal of identifying new biomarkers (bacterial signatures) to reduce the risk of APOs. 

  • Population and Public Health: We perform comprehensive omics analysis on large, country-based cohorts to address pressing health challenges.  We seek to bridge the gap between discovery science and public health impact by generating meaningful and actionable data that is not only scientifically valuable but also actionable (guiding policies, interventions and health care decisions and informing Sustainable Development Goals, SDGs). In addition, our work enables discovery sciences by opening opportunities for new biological insights and future scientific breakthroughs.

  • Infectious Diseases: We aim to study infectious diseases using cutting-edge genomics approaches to better understand how pathogens emerge, spread and affect populations. Our work focuses on pathogen discovery, genomic epidemiology and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Through whole genome sequencing and bioinformatics, we can identify novel or re-emerging pathogens. These insights can inform outbreak preparedness and response strategies.

data.title: About the group
data.body:
The Bone and Mineral Disease Research Group (BMDRG), founded in 2007 within the Section of Chemical Pathology at Aga Khan University, is dedicated to advancing metabolic medicine through clinical, biochemical, and molecular research. In 2012, it formally articulated its objectives, evolving into a multidisciplinary team addressing the rising burden of metabolic bone diseases in Pakistan.

Initial work focused on documenting disease patterns through clinical observations and retrospective reviews. This expanded into community-based surveys exploring determinants of vitamin D deficiency and osteoporosis, leading to the development of population-specific tools. The group has investigated key biomarkers, including parathyroid hormone, bone turnover markers, FGF23, and anti-CCP, with special attention to high-risk groups such as patients with rheumatologic disorders, thalassemia, chronic kidney disease, and parathyroid conditions. Clinical trials have further evaluated vitamin D supplementation strategies, pharmacologic therapies, and surgical interventions.

Education and training remain central pillars. Initiatives include courses on bone densitometry, osteoporosis, fracture liaison service training, and the development of risk assessment tools and clinical practice guidelines. Expanding its vision, BMDRG launched the Fragility Fracture Network Pakistan (FFN-Pak) in 2021.

Recognized by IOF, APCO, and the Global FFN, the group now aspires to establish a Center of Excellence in Bone, Mineral, and Musculoskeletal Disorders, aligning with SDG Goal 3: Good Health and Well-Being. In the next three years, we envision advancing bone and mineral health through innovation, precision, and collaboration—integrating machine learning, genomics, and biomarker research to pioneer precision medicine in metabolic bone and rare skeletal disorders.

Webpage updated May 2026

data.title: Aims and Objectives
data.body:
The group seeks to build on and sustain the progress of its earlier work through the following objectives:

  • Implementation of Guidelines: Translate evidence into practice by implementing clinical guidelines in collaboration with the Center of Clinical Best Practices, using the Re-AIM framework, with a focus on osteoporosis, thalassemia, and vitamin D–related disorders.

  • Fracture Liaison Service (FLS): Establish and implement a comprehensive FLS program to ensure effective secondary prevention of fractures.

New Objectives

  • Guideline Development: Formulate new evidence-based guidelines for parathyroid disorders and hypophosphatemic conditions.

  • Rare Skeletal Disorders: Expand research and clinical focus to rare skeletal disorders, with special emphasis on hypophosphatemic osteomalacia and renal tubular disorders.​

data.title: Research Themes
data.body:
Theme

Advancing Bone and Mineral Health through Innovation, Precision, and Collaboration

Focus Areas

  • Machine Learning and Data Science: Harnessing artificial intelligence and advanced analytics to improve disease prediction, risk stratification, and personalized treatment pathways in bone and mineral disorders.

  • Rare Skeletal Disorders: Expanding research into under-recognized and complex conditions, with a focus on hypophosphatemic osteomalacia, renal tubular disorders, and other rare skeletal diseases.

  • Precision Medicine: Integrating genomics, biomarkers, and patient-specific data to tailor diagnosis, prevention, and therapy for metabolic bone and mineral disorders.

  • Clinical Translation and Implementation Science: Developing and applying guidelines, best practices, and innovative care models such as fracture liaison services, aligned with the Re-AIM framework, to ensure real-world impact.

  • Education and Capacity Building: Training healthcare professionals in bone health, metabolic medicine, and advanced diagnostics, fostering the next generation of clinician-scientists in this field.

  • Male bone health: Advance understanding of male osteoporosis and men’s bone health through local research

data.title: Engagement and Involvement: Public and private
data.body:
​​Organizing Various Events

  1. As an activity on World Osteoporosis Day 2024, the 1st International Osteoporosis and Bone Health Summit was held on October 22, 2024, in Karachi. The summit featured key insights from renowned professionals including Prof. Kassim Javaid and Prof. Michael F. Holick from the UK, Dr. Aysha Habib, Dr. Hafsa Majid, Dr. Tashfeen Ahmad and Dr. Masood Umer from Aga Khan University, Dr. Shahid Noor from Liaquat National Hospital, and other leading experts.

  2. Dr. Khadija Irfan, President of Punja Chapter of FFN-Pakistan led a quality-improvement study by the Asia Pacific Consortium on Osteoporosis (APCO) "Evaluating Compliance with the Care Standard of Proactively Assessing Bone Health in Patients with Diabetes" from the Department of Endocrinology and Metabolism, Services Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan. The study identified challenges in bone health screening and recommended structured software system to implement evidence-based protocols incorporating mandatory, stepwise history-taking, examination, and data entry for ensuring standardized assessment and reliable data.

  3. A course on osteoporosis was conducted by the International Society for Clinical Densitometry in collaboration with FFN-Pakistan's Punjab Chapter on 19th July 2025. The course participants were from many cities in Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and included doctors managing fragility fractures and radiologists dealing with DEXA.

  4. The 2nd International Osteoporosis and Bone Health Conference  was organized in Lahore by the Punjab Chapter of FFN Pakistan on 18th December 2024. The highlight of the event was the insightful keynote addresses by Prof. Michael F. Hollick from the UK and Prof. Faisal Masood from Lahore. Panel discussions featured esteemed professors from medicine, endocrinology, gynecology, and orthopedics, creating a rich multidisciplinary dialogue. A lively question-and-answer session fostered meaningful interaction, allowing both experts and the general public to engage directly with the speakers. The conference concluded with a forward-looking discussion collaborative, evidence-based osteoporosis prevention and treatment.

data.title: About the group
data.body: ​In 2018, the Breast Program Leadership Committee (BPLC)was formed, which brought together a closely knit multidisciplinary team that was representative of their specialities. One of the areas of focus at this forum (BPLC) has been enhancing institutional research and collaboration with local and international partners. In 2020, we started a monthly breast research group meeting for all to share ideas and have an opportunity for peer review. With this success, we feel it is now time to formalize the group to facilitate collaborative projects. ​

data.title: Aims and Objectives
data.body: ​To build a platform where a multidisciplinary team can bring together their academic strengths to answer key research questions related to breast cancer and other breast related disorders in our population. We plan to perform and publish research in clinical as well as basic science, that would not only help us address issues that are relevant to our setup and population, but also beyond our borders and the region.​

data.title: About the group
data.body: ​In 2017, likeminded people from within and outside the Department of Emergency Medicine at the Aga Khan University Hospital created an interest group for sudden cardiac Arrest . The group’s ultimate goal was to improve the rate of survival in these patients, especially those suffering from Out of Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA). Although everyone in the group had been working towards that goal even prior to formation of the group, the synergy created by coming together was particularly evident for increased rate of by-stander Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) as an integral part in saving lives of OHCA patients.

data.title: About the group
data.body:
The idea for this development came from Dr. Vellani’s observation of changes in the QRS waveform with ST depression occurred together during exercise tolerance test in patients with single vessel stenosis. Measurements of the voltages and directions of averaged 30-80 QRS waveforms at each stage of exercise formed the basis of the analysis of electrical vectors for detection of ischemia. 

Software was developed at AKU to analyse orthogonal ECG signals with minimal noise, to provide an averaged lead signal representative of each stage of exercise.  Orthogonal planar vectors derived from these signals enabled measurement of changes in magnitude and direction of the resultant vectors. The method of data acquisition during exercise and analysis of electrical vectors has been patented in the USA and Pakistan. 

Reduction in progression of the voltages of depolarization vectors indicated the region of ischemia and its spatial orientation. Compared with myocardial perfusion scan the sensitivity and specificity of detection of ischemia by changes in vectors in 114 patients were 88% and 71%, respectively. 

Correlation with coronary angiography will establish the accuracy and limitations of the method. Trial of the exercise test for ischemia in service will be done with high resolution data acquisition equipment currently under construction. ​​

data.title: Aims and Objectives
data.body:
• To develop a system for recording high-resolution ECG signals during exercise that contain minimal artefact without the use of filters, in order to identify changes in electrical vectors that indicate myocardial ischaemia, for use in a health service.
  • To determine the accuracy of electrical vectors for detection, location and severity of stenosis of coronary arteries shown by coronary angiography.
  • To determine the relation of physical work units with the detection of ischaemia and the extent of coronary stenosis.
  • To determine whether the absence of ischaemia indicated by electrical vectors during stress is associated with less than 50% stenosis of a coronary artery. 
  • To assess the value and feasibility of using the system for analysis of electrical vectors during exercise for clinical decisions.

data.body: Reliable cost-effective, widely accessible exercise test for detection and location of inducible myocardial ischaemia.​​

data.title: About the group
data.body:
​Like other developing countries, there has been a rapid increase in cardiovascular diseases. Consequently, the cost of treatment and mortalities pose a significant burden to individuals and their care givers. Taking these observations into consideration, a preventive programme was initiated by the institution in the form of SMART heart programme.

This programme sets the stage for population-based research on cardio-metabolic disorders, and resources that were developed for implementation of this programme. The research group includes Dr. Khawar Kazmi and Dr. Romaina Iqbal, both of whom have been involved in multiple landmark studies including the Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology (“PURE”) study.

The formation of this research group will strengthen the structure of research collaboration within different disciplines and departments. With this effort, the group will be able to work more closely towards their common interest and obtain support from the university for their research work.

  • Develop algorithm to detect, educate and control  hypertension in rural and urban , population and integrate health care plan using mhealth technology
  • Study prevalence and predictors of childhood obesity and conduct school based health interventions to reduce the risk of childhood obesity

data.title: About the group
data.body:
​Child abuse and violence is rapidly emerging as one of the most pressing social issues for Pakistan. Such crimes are tragic reminders of the failure to provide secure environment to our children and they call for a complete overhaul of our intent towards child protection. 

With the ultimate goal to build/develop the ideal child protection team, we have initiated our efforts at a smaller scale with people from within and outside of AKU. The members of this group were already involved in the area of child abuse prevention and child protection, hence their respective experiences allowed natural synergies. The stakeholders of this group are diverse: ranging from department of paediatrics, nursing, child psychology and psychiatry, department of emergency medicine, to department of community Health Sciences.

Thus, together, the group has generated a number of ideas ranging from primary to secondary prevention. We shall soon embark on a long term, more comprehensive phase delving into child abuse prevention, recognition and intervention.

data.title: About the group
data.body:
​Dr Fadoo, AKU graduate and pediatric oncologist, have been affiliated with AKU for the last 20 years. Dr. Fadoo has been working fulltime, as Pediatric Oncologist and now serving as Chair Department of Oncology. Over the last 2 decades has been working to improve the outcome of childhood cancer in Pakistan. Childhood ALL, the most common childhood cancer, was the priority. She started their first multi-institutional study (never previously done in Pakistan) in 2009, prospectively recruiting and following children with ALL in three institutions in Karachi. The findings were published and created a topic of debate as some characteristics were distinct from those published in other populations. We believe further study is needed, especially at the molecular and genetic level to validate these clinical findings and potentially impact survival. 

Dr Ghias, a cancer biologist, was an ideal addition to this team. The group collaborates and has completed a transitional research study on AML with Sidra Medicine, Qatar. A further plan to study children with various types of leukemia to help understand the particular biology of the disease in Pakistan and other clinical and socio-economic factors that may interact in impacting treatment outcome.

​Dr Azhar is a cancer biologist with extensive experience in basic science research on identifying aberrant signaling and apoptotic pathways in cancer. His work on identifying disruption of the apoptotic pathways in Burkitt’s lymphoma as well as targeting dysregulated pathways in leukemia and lymphoma got him the HRH Princess Adilah Bint Abdullah Humanitarian and Research award in Children Cancer, Riyadh in 2010. In addition to childhood cancers, Dr Hussain has also worked extensively on adult solid tumors such as breast, colorectal, thyroid and ovarian cancers.

data.title: Goals & Objectives
data.body:
The main objective of Cardiology residency program is to produce knowledgeable and skilled cardiologists, who at the end of their training are able to:
  • Independently manage  routine and complex acute and chronic adult cardiac problems
  • Diagnose routine pediatric cardiac problems and start initial management
  • Manage ambulatory cardiac patients independently
  • Teach/educate students, interns and residents, ancillary staff and patients
  • Learn and practice preventive cardiology
  • Manage pre- and post-operative cardiac and hemodynamic complications in cardiac and non-cardiac surgical patients
  • Independently perform and interpret non-invasive cardiac diagnostic procedures, e.g. ETT, Echo, Stress echo, trans-esophageal echo (TEE), ambulatory blood pressure (ABPM), ECG monitoring (Holter) and nuclear cardiac imaging
  • Independently perform central line insertion with bedside hemodynamic monitoring, temporary pacemaker insertion, and peri-cardiocentesis
  • Independently perform right and left heart catheterization
  • Observe and assist in coronary, valvular interventions, electrophysiological studies/ablations and device implantation
  • Understand the basic principles of research; design and conduct of a study to the final stages of manuscript writing and publication
  • Devote extended (elective) time in an area of interest and/or acquire in-depth skills in nuclear cardiology, stress echo, trans-esophageal echo, cardiac electrophysiology and cardiac intervention at AKU and other centers of excellence.

data.title: Duration and Outline of Training
data.body: The selected candidates are required to undergo a comprehensive training for a period of three years. Rotations are in accordance with the rules of the College of Physicians and Surgeons, Pakistan.   • Eligible to appear in Medicine Intermediate Module examination (IMM) or FCPS (Medicine) examination conducted by CPSP. Candidates holding FCPS (Medicine) or equivalent diploma may have preference.

data.body:
Goals

The primary goal of the programme is to develop Public Health experts with a comprehensive knowledge of the sciences of Community Medicine and the skills and competence to apply this knowledge to a broad range of community health issues in the socio-economic, cultural, political and ethical context.

Objectives

At the end of the training, residents should be able to:
  • Develop, implement and evaluate effective public health interventions and programmes in Pakistan and the developing world.
  • Educate medical undergraduates and graduates and other health workers in the practice of public health.
  • Develop and conduct research on public health issues.
  • Deliver effective preventive and curative care including systematically improving quality of health care at first level care in rural and urban areas.
  • Pursue continuous and self-directed professional learning to update and expand their knowledge and skills.

  • Practice of public health at a local, regional, national or international level.
  • Planning and administration of health services.
  • Clinical practice in community settings.
  • The assessment and control of locally endemic health problems.
  • Teaching undergraduate and postgraduate students and other health workers.
  • Research in Public Health and Medicine.

data.title: Duration and Outline of Training
data.body:
The four years of training broadly covers three domains:

Academic:  A resident has to take part in academic activities throughout the residency programme. The residency programme offers core curriculum modules, journal club and PGME core lectures and workshops throughout the training period.

Research:  Research domain is spread over the four years of residency, starting from year 1 when trainees are required to develop and submit their synopsis to CPSP. In next 3 years, a resident has to complete dissertation, do internal and external placements in any public health domain, contribute in data analysis, and write up activities. During the four years of training, residents rotate through the five sections within CHS to get a comprehensive understanding of the specific public health domains, including Population & Reproductive Health, Epidemiology & Biostatistics & Infectious Diseases, Environmental & Occupational Health & Injuries, Health Policy & Management, and Non-communicable Diseases. 

Service:  Service component comprises rotation in various clinical departments across the hospital, and outside in the community. Clinical rotations are in accordance​ with the College of Physicians and Surgeons Pakistan (CPSP) requirements. A resident has to do clinics and conduct health education sessions in field-based settings, in CHS Urban and Rural Health Programmes. Teaching is an essential component of the training programme and each resident has to teach at the undergraduate level and various Continuing Education Programme (CEP) short courses. Residents also contribute to various public health service-related activities as part of their sectional rotation described above.

data.body:
This is a four-year programme, and the residents are trained through rotations in different sections of radiology, which are in accordance with the CPSP guidelines.

data.title: On-call Duties and Reporting Time
data.body:
Emergency in-house calls are part of the training programme. Call system during residency grooms the residents to become responsible in-patient care.  Adequate supervision of faculty and senior residents help the juniors to flourish with confidence.

The aim of on-call duty is to provide effective radiological coverage for the management of emergencies after working hours in the ER or the wards. The second important aim is the exposure of residents to emergency radiologic problems and their independent handling.

data.title: Goals and Objectives
data.body:
Goals

The principal goal of the diagnostic radiology residency programme is to meet and surpass the requirements of the College of Physicians and Surgeons Pakistan (CPSP), provide high-quality training to support the development of competent, caring radiologists who possess the knowledge, skills and capabilities necessary to:
  • Pass the board examinations given by CPSP.
  • Pursue a fellowship, enter private practice or begin an academic career
  • Practice radiology according to the standards set by the Postgraduate Medical Education (PGME), CPSP and other professional organizations
  • Practice lifelong learning so they will be able to continually discover new knowledge in radiology
  • Serve their patients and community in which they practice as competent professionals
Objectives

The objective of the radiology residency of Aga Khan University (AKU) is to empower the naïve learner to become an independent consultant whose quest for research, leadership qualities and empathy had been revived by a dynamic and structured process. All this is accomplished while fostering individual talents and qualities.
